newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition wary of Serbian government "retreat'.
newsitem.headline: Opposition wary of Serbian government "retreat'.

text.p: An apparent Serbian government climbdown in a marathon dispute over annulled local elections provoked opposition scepticism and vows to press on with mass demonstrations for democratic reform.
Tens of thousands of protesters massed in Belgrade and other cities on Saturday, the 55th straight day of street rallies, even after apparent acquiesence by senior government ministers.

Serbian deputy prime ministers Ratko Markovic and Nedeljko Sipovac and a delegation of Belgrade University students representing the protest coalition issued a joint statement after a meeting on Saturday calling for "genuine and final" results in the November local elections won by the opposition movement to be honoured.

Senior political sources said President Slobodan Milosevic was planning shakeups in the cabinet, the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) and the state-run media as well as offering government posts to the opposition to defuse popular pressure.
Opposition election victories in 14 of Serbia's 18 largest cities including the capital Belgrade and second largest city Nis were cancelled by the SPS over alleged "irregularities".

An Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) inquiry declared the elections valid and Western governments have demanded that Milosevic comply with the verdict or forget about financial aid needed by Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia to rebuild its economy.
Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, said on Saturday night the deputy prime ministers' statement was "a belated step toward reason".

But he and other Zajedno leaders accused Milosevic of scheming to outmanoeuvre the opposition with "piecemeal concessions" that would not jeopardise the decades-old authoritarian grip of the SPS in the end.
They ruled out Zajedno joining any SPS-led government.
The hardline SPS city board in Nis gave room for opposition suspicions by rejecting a Serbian Justice Ministry finding last week that Zajedno had won the voting in that city after all.
The statement released by the deputy prime ministers in conjunction with the students did not mention Zajedno or state that the SPS had lost or doctored the November 17 balloting.

But political analysts said the statement appeared to tacitly admit that the decision to annul the outcome was wrong, which would clear the way for election commissions to reinstate Zajedno victories on orders from Belgrade.

"The Serbian government representatives agreed with the necessity that the will of the citizens expressed at local elections must be fully respected," the statement signed by the deputy premiers and the students said.
"Their stands and ours are identical on (our) demands," Cedomir Jovanovic, a student protest leader, told Reuters.

A separate student statement said Markovic and Sipovac demanded that "competent ministries make public the genuine and final results as soon as possible and (state) that the government will accept them".

Several district chapters of the Yugoslav United Left (JUL), a party allied with the SPS and led by Milosevic's neo-communist wife, said they backed efforts to "correct errors and omissions" in the election process.

Belgrade Mayor Nebojsa Covic, a prominent SPS moderate dismayed by his party's loss of credibility, told student Radio Index that he also wanted the election results respected and perpetrators of fraud prosecuted.

He said he had refused to constitute a new Belgrade municipal assembly so far because it was "appointed in a way against which tens of thousands of students and Belgraders have been demonstrating for two months now".
Serbia faces parliamentary and then presidential elections by the end of this year.
